title: Integral base change on the source
statement:
Let $f:X\to S$ and $n\geq1$ invertible on $S$ be as in [sbc-def-base-change-property], and let $q\geq1$. Consider a commutative diagram of schemes
$$
\begin{array}{ccccccc}
X & \xleftarrow{} & X\prime & \xleftarrow{\pi\prime} & X\prime\prime & \xleftarrow{h\prime} & Y\\
f\downarrow && f\prime\downarrow && f\prime\prime\downarrow && e\downarrow\\
S & \xleftarrow{} & S\prime & \xleftarrow{\pi} & S\prime\prime & \xleftarrow{g\prime} & T
\end{array}
$$
whose three squares are Cartesian [sbc-def-base-change-square]. Put $h=\pi\prime\circ h\prime:Y\to X\prime$ and $g=\pi\circ g\prime:T\to S\prime$. Assume $g\prime$ is quasi-compact and quasi-separated [def-weil-pbc-scheme-conventions] and $\pi$ is integral [def-weil-finite-integral-morphism]. Let $\mathcal F$ be an abelian sheaf on $T_{\mathrm{Et}}$ annihilated by $n$. If the degree-$q$ base-change map [sbc-def-base-change-map]
$$
f\prime{}^{-1}R^qg_*\mathcal F\longrightarrow R^qh_*e^{-1}\mathcal F
$$
is an isomorphism, then the degree-$q$ base-change map
$$
f\prime\prime{}^{-1}R^qg\prime_*\mathcal F\longrightarrow R^qh\prime_*e^{-1}\mathcal F
$$
is an isomorphism. No base-change hypothesis on $f$ and no surjectivity hypothesis on $\pi$ is required.

proof.text: The middle square identifies $\pi\prime:X\prime\prime\to X\prime$ as a base change of $\pi:S\prime\prime\to S\prime$, so it is integral by [lem-sbc-integral-morphism-base-change]. Thus [sbc-lem-integral-etale-direct-image-exact] applies to both $\pi$ and $\pi\prime$: their direct images on abelian etale sheaves are exact, and their bounded-below derived direct images are their termwise direct images.

Apply [lem-sbc-integral-underived-exchange] with coefficient ring $\mathbf Z$ to the middle square, with integral direct-image map $\pi$, its base change $\pi\prime$, and inverse-image map $f\prime$. It gives the canonical isomorphism $f\prime{}^{-1}\pi_*\cong\pi\prime_*f\prime\prime{}^{-1}$. Since the two direct images are exact, every complex computes their derived functors by [lem-weil-pbc-exact-functor-derived-functor]. Apply the underived exchange termwise: its components commute with differentials by naturality and are isomorphisms in every degree. Its derived map is the derived exchange of [sbc-def-base-change-map], as follows. For a bounded-below complex $K$, choose a resolution $K\to I$. Exactness makes $\pi_*K\to\pi_*I$ and $\pi\prime_*f\prime\prime{}^{-1}K\to\pi\prime_*f\prime\prime{}^{-1}I$ quasi-isomorphisms. Naturality of underived exchange gives the commutative square with these two comparison maps as its vertical sides and the exchanges at $K$ and $I$ as its horizontal sides. All inverse images here are the exact termwise functors specified in [sbc-def-base-change-map]. The adjunctions $\pi^{-1}\dashv\pi_*$ and $\pi\prime{}^{-1}\dashv\pi\prime_*$ therefore descend termwise; their units and counits are the images of the sheaf units and counits. The transpose of the exchange at $I$ is explicitly $\pi\prime{}^{-1}f\prime{}^{-1}\pi_*I\cong f\prime\prime{}^{-1}\pi^{-1}\pi_*I\xrightarrow{f\prime\prime{}^{-1}\varepsilon_\pi}f\prime\prime{}^{-1}I$. Localizing this transpose is precisely the derived transpose in [sbc-def-base-change-map], so the commutative comparison square identifies the termwise exchange with that specified derived map. Hence the derived exchange $\alpha:f\prime{}^{-1}R\pi_*\to R\pi\prime_*f\prime\prime{}^{-1}$ is an isomorphism, in particular at $Rg\prime_*\mathcal F$.

Let $\beta:f\prime\prime{}^{-1}Rg\prime_*\mathcal F\to Rh\prime_*e^{-1}\mathcal F$ be the inner derived base-change map. Apply the vertical-pasting equation, clause (3) of [lem-weil-pbc-exchange-identity-pasting], to the square of $\pi$ and the square of $g\prime$. The exchanged-square convention identifies the outer map with
$$f\prime{}^{-1}R(\pi g\prime)_*\mathcal F\ \cong\ f\prime{}^{-1}R\pi_*Rg\prime_*\mathcal F\ \xrightarrow{\alpha}\ R\pi\prime_*f\prime\prime{}^{-1}Rg\prime_*\mathcal F\ \xrightarrow{R\pi\prime_*\beta}\ R\pi\prime_*Rh\prime_*e^{-1}\mathcal F\ \cong\ R(\pi\prime h\prime)_*e^{-1}\mathcal F.$$
The composition isomorphisms are exactly those in that cited equation. By [sbc-def-base-change-map] the degree-$q$ maps are the cohomology of these derived maps. Because $\pi\prime_*$ is exact, [lem-weil-pbc-exact-functor-complex-cohomology] identifies $H^q(R\pi\prime_*\beta)$ naturally with $\pi\prime_*H^q(\beta)$. Consequently, up to the displayed isomorphisms and $H^q(\alpha)$, the outer degree-$q$ map is $\pi\prime_*b$, where $b=H^q(\beta)$ is the desired inner degree-$q$ map. The assumed isomorphism of the outer map therefore implies that $\pi\prime_*b$ is an isomorphism.

Exactness of $\pi\prime_*$ gives $\pi\prime_*\ker b=\ker(\pi\prime_*b)=0$ and $\pi\prime_*\operatorname{coker}b=\operatorname{coker}(\pi\prime_*b)=0$, since the latter map is an isomorphism. Apply [lem-sbc-integral-direct-image-detects-zero] to each of these sheaves, again with coefficient ring $\mathbf Z$ and integral map $\pi\prime$. It yields $\ker b=0$ and $\operatorname{coker}b=0$. In the abelian category of abelian etale sheaves a map with zero kernel and cokernel is an isomorphism, so $b$ is an isomorphism as claimed. No surjectivity of $\pi$ was used.

blueprint_update.statement:
With $f:X\to S$ and $n$ as in [sbc-def-base-change-property] and some
$q\geq1$, consider
commutative
diagrams

$$
\begin{array}{ccccccc}
X & \xleftarrow{\;\;} & X' & \xleftarrow{\pi'} & X'' & &
Y\\
f\big\downarrow & & \big\downarrow f' & & \big\downarrow f'' & &
\big\downarrow e\\
S & \xleftarrow{\;\;} & S' & \xleftarrow{\;\pi\;} & S'' & &
T
\end{array}
$$

and the diagram with the outer
$h=h'\circ\pi''$, $g=g'\circ\pi$ (as horizontal composites), all squares
Cartesian, $g'$ quasi-compact and quasi-separated, and $\pi$ integral.
Let $\mathcal F$ be an abelian sheaf on $T_{\Et}$ annihilated by $n$.
If

$$
f'^{-1}R^qg_*\mathcal F\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }R^qh_*e^{-1}\mathcal F
$$

is an isomorphism, then
$f''^{-1}R^qg'_*\mathcal F\to R^qh'_*e^{-1}\mathcal F$ is an
isomorphism.

proof.text:
Since $\pi$ and $\pi'$ are integral, $\pi_*$ and $\pi'_*$ are exact
by [sbc-lem-integral-etale-direct-image-exact] (finite case
[lemma-weil-pbc-finite-direct-image-exact]) and
$(f')^{-1}\pi_*=\pi'_*(f'')^{-1}$, so
$\pi'_*(f'')^{-1}R^qg'_*\mathcal F=(f')^{-1}R^qg_*\mathcal F$ and
$\pi'_*R^qh'_*e^{-1}\mathcal F=R^qh_*e^{-1}\mathcal F$; hence the
assumption says that the map for $f''$ becomes an isomorphism after
$\pi'_*$. It remains to see that the exact functor $\pi'_*$ is conservative;
apply it to the kernel and cokernel $\mathcal C$ of that map, so
$\pi'_*\mathcal C=0$. Let $\bar x''$ be a geometric point of $X''$ and
$\bar x'$ its image. The stalk $(\pi'_*\mathcal C)_{\bar x'}$ is
$\Gamma(\operatorname{Spec}B,\mathcal C)$ with
$B$ the ring of
$X''\times_{X'}\operatorname{Spec}\mathcal O^{\mathrm{sh}}_{X',\bar x'}$ over an
affine neighbourhood, an integral algebra over the strictly henselian ring
$A=\mathcal O^{\mathrm{sh}}_{X',\bar x'}$. Write $B=\operatorname{colim}B_\lambda$
with $B_\lambda$ finite over $A$; each $B_\lambda$ is a finite product of
strictly henselian local rings, so sections over $\operatorname{Spec}B_\lambda$
are the product of the stalks at their closed points, and the stalk
$\mathcal C_{\bar x''}$ is the colimit of the factors through which
$\bar x''$ passes. Hence $\mathcal C_{\bar x''}$ is a quotient of
$(\pi'_*\mathcal C)_{\bar x'}=0$, so $\mathcal C=0$. No surjectivity of
$\pi$ is needed, and the map for $f''$ is an isomorphism.
